fact: A primary head teacher trained on the School Information System in Handeni says that a pupil marked absent three times in a row triggers a message sent straight to the parent, so attendance is marked per learner in the system; the council's education officer says teachers are to start entering their schools' information at once.

Handeni Town Council trained head teachers of primary schools, heads of secondary schools and one teacher from each school on the School Information System on 9 January 2026, to use it from the reopening of schools.

The Handeni education officer says the Prime Minister's Office (TAMISEMI) has directed that the School Information System come into official use when schools open on 13 January 2026, with the council to follow up regularly.
Head teachers in Handeni Town Council were trained on the School Information System on 9 January 2026, ahead of the official start of use directed by TAMISEMI for 13 January 2026.

The report gives no number of schools trained or using the School Information System in Handeni Town Council or nationally; it says one teacher per school and every head was trained on 9 January 2026.
The head teacher of Mshikamano Primary School in Handeni says that before the School Information System the school kept its data on paper, which was sometimes lost or damaged.

The Citizen reports on 18 November 2025 that the government is preparing to introduce a student-tracking system following each learner from early childhood to higher education, to verify numbers and identify pupils who repeat, drop out or transfer, according to the education ministry's Permanent Secretary, Prof Carolyne Nombo; no start date is given.

The planned student-tracking system is announced by the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology as the ministry's own, with the government exploring registration of children at birth to feed it; the article gives no date beyond its own, 18 November 2025.

As of the article's date, 18 November 2025, the student-tracking system is described as being prepared and not yet introduced at any level; a researcher quoted says Tanzania lacks real-time tracking of learners.
The article of 18 November 2025 names no school using the planned student-tracking system, which the government is still preparing to introduce.

The Rural Youth Collective reports that in every five schools it surveyed in Mbeya District Council in August 2025 only one had a single teacher with a basic understanding of EMIS, none formally trained; it gives no number of schools surveyed and no count of schools entering data.
The Rural Youth Collective's August 2025 investigation in Mbeya District Council covered primary and secondary schools, whose teachers are expected to record and submit data through EMIS.

The investigation describes EMIS in rural Mbeya schools in August 2025 as digital systems designed to track student attendance and examination results, which teachers are expected to use daily and through which parents should be able to see their children's progress; it also says teachers untrained in them cannot properly record and submit data, and does not say what is actually entered.
